phrases.text: Around midnight on 13 August 1961,
the signal went out in East Berlin.
Erich Honecker, who had been preparing the operation in strict secrecy,
gave the word alarm.
The operation was carried out under the protection
of armed units of the East German army,
the People's Police and the factory combat groups,
and the sector border was sealed off.
Picture that border on the night it was closed.
The building of the Wall began that day.
The four occupying powers still held rights in this city.
So the question for this episode is simple.
How could one side close a border through the middle of
Berlin while those rights were still in place?
Those rights rest on the four-power status of Berlin.
In the October standoff that followed, the Americans, invoking that status,
insisted on their right to move freely throughout the city,
according to the Stiftung Berliner Mauer. In the summer of 1961
the Western reply to the closure was narrower.
The federal agency for civic education, the bpb,
says the Western Allies limited themselves to verbal protests and demonstrative acts.
The protests were made, the Wall was built anyway, and the
crossings became the place where the argument moved onto the street.
You can still walk that street today.
The bpb's chronicle of 1961 records that on 19 August Vice President
Lyndon Johnson and General Lucius Clay were sent to Berlin.
The bpb calls Clay the popular Hero of the Blockade.
The State Department's historical record gives Clay's position in precise terms.
From August 1961, he was President Kennedy's special representative in Berlin,
with the rank of ambassador.
He was the President's representative on the spot.
Keep that role in mind. From here on,
the story is less about the Wall itself than about who was
allowed to cross the line in front of it,
and who decided what happened when someone tried.
Now walk to the crossing itself.
Checkpoint Charlie stood where Friedrichstraße meets Zimmerstraße.
The Chronik der Mauer, the online chronicle of the Wall,
places the tank confrontation of October 1961 at that junction,
and says about four million people from all
over the world visit the site every year.
The same chronicle says the Western Allies used
the crossing to show their presence and to underline
their right to access all sectors of the city.
The American side saw its personnel as holding
rights under the four-power status of the city.
The East German border police applied the rules of
the East German state. Where those two positions met,
a single car could be stopped in the street.
On 22 October 1961, Allan Lightner, a senior American diplomat,
set out with his wife for the opera in East Berlin.
The Stiftung Berliner Mauer records that East German border police asked him
to identify himself at the crossing, and that he refused.
Wikipedia's account of the crisis says he was stopped while crossing at
Checkpoint Charlie, and the two accounts agree on the core.
A senior diplomat was stopped at the line,
and he would not identify himself to the guards.
For the Americans this was not a minor matter.
The Soviet side had its own view of the rules,
and each side held that its position was the correct one.
Lightner did not give up, and neither did the American side.
According to the Stiftung's account, he got across nearly two hours later,
escorted by American military police in two jeeps with eight armed men.
The convoy had been turned back twice before
the third attempt went through without a stop.
The Americans strongly protested to the Soviet Union,
invoking the four-power status of the city.
The Soviets answered by citing a regulation of the East German Interior
Ministry, which said that Western Allies in civilian clothes must identify
themselves when they wished to cross the border.
So the dispute was never only about one car.
It was about a rule that one side would not accept
and the other said it was simply enforcing.
Picture the scene in the street:
the convoy stopping, turning round and trying again.
The next two days followed the same pattern.
The Stiftung Berliner Mauer says the situation was
repeated over and over again on Friedrichstraße.
East German border police stopped American personnel in civilian clothes,
and armed American military police arrived to escort them through the crossing.
Each refusal tested the arrangements that the Western
powers believed still held in Berlin.
The Stiftung says the Americans turned to harsher measures on 25 October.
The Stiftung describes the same routine for each attempt:
the stop, the refusal and the armed escort.
On 25 October the Americans brought tanks to the crossing.
The Stiftung's account gives the numbers: ten tanks,
three driven up to the border on Friedrichstraße and seven stationed on
either side of the street, directly next to the Wall.
Only that account gives these numbers, so they are attributed to it.
That evening the tanks withdrew.
The next afternoon they came back for about an hour.
A dispute about papers had become a matter for tanks,
and the Soviet side would have to decide how to answer.
The Americans had shown what they would do.
The next question was what the other side would do.
The Americans had shown that they would send tanks,
and the East German border police had shown that they would keep
asking for papers. Neither side had yet answered
the question the other had put to it.
The sources do not show that the border guards' rule was changed.
What would the Soviets do the next time
the Americans came back to the crossing?
That answer came in the late afternoon of 27 October,
on the same stretch of Friedrichstraße,
and it turned an argument over papers into a standoff between tanks.
How far would it go, and who would decide?
Quick break. I'm Yusuf, and this is Walk of Berlin.
If you enjoy stories like this one,
come and walk one with me.
My walk, Berlin Then and Now,
goes from the World Clock on Alexanderplatz to Hackescher Markt,
with an archive photo at every stop.
You'll find it at walk of berlin dot com.
On 27 October the Soviet side answered.
The Stiftung says the American tanks had been alerted and returned to
Checkpoint Charlie, and then ten Soviet tanks drove up
to the East Berlin side of the crossing for the first time.
Shortly after six in the evening, the two sides faced each other
in a menacing standoff in the middle of Berlin.
The State Department's historical record gives the same outline from another angle.
It says the Soviet tanks advanced up Friedrichstraße late in the afternoon.
Two sources, two slightly different starting times, and one picture:
tanks on a city street, facing each other.
The number did not stay at ten.
By midnight, according to the State Department's record,
the number of Soviet tanks had grown to thirty.
The standoff ran through the night and into the morning.
The Stiftung and the record both describe ten Soviet tanks at the
start, and this episode uses the record's count of thirty for midnight.
Today you can walk the same street on foot.
The tanks that stood there in October 1961 are gone,
and only the record of that night remains.
The accounts agree on the main shape of the
standoff and differ on some of the smaller details,
so this episode keeps to the points they share.
General Clay answered the standoff in public.
The State Department's record describes a press conference he held at
Berlin Command shortly after the Soviet tanks appeared.
It says he announced that the Soviet tanks' appearance clearly indicated
who was responsible for harassing American officials trying to enter East Berlin.
The record gives that statement in its own paraphrase,
so the wording here is the record's,
not a direct quotation from Clay.
The same record says that President Kennedy called
Clay that evening to review the situation.
It cites the historian Cates for the call,
and notes that no other record of that conversation has been found.
The public statement is on the record.
The telephone call rests on one historian's account,
so read it as a single source.
Who gave the order to move the Soviet tanks forward?
The State Department's record does not say.
It describes Clay's press conference and the President's call,
and it does not identify who decided on the Soviet advance.
The tanks are easy to picture,
because they were there on the street.
The decisions behind them are much harder to see,
and the sources are thinner on them than on the tanks.
That gap is part of this story.
Anyone on the street could see the armour,
but the decisions were being made elsewhere,
through channels the people at the crossing could not see.
No one standing on the street could see how this would end.
The answer was being shaped through a channel that had little
to do with the uniforms on either side of the crossing.
Wikipedia says that Robert Kennedy and Georgi Bolshakov's discussions helped bring
about the understanding that led to the pullback.
The State Department's editorial note also links
Bolshakov to the attorney general, Robert Kennedy,
and cites Peter Wyden's book Wall for the attorney general's account.
The record quotes that account from Peter Wyden's book,
and it notes that no archive document supports or refutes it.
The two sources name the same channel.
The State Department's editorial note sets out two accounts, and they differ.
In the first, which comes from Khrushchev's memoirs,
Khrushchev ordered the Soviet tanks to pull back in
order to save American face. In the second,
the attorney general says the President asked him to contact Bolshakov and
use that channel to get the tanks removed, and Bolshakov agreed.
The note is careful about what this proves.
It says that no document at the Kennedy Library or in
the State Department's records supports or refutes either account.
Neither account can be checked against the archives,
which is the note's own point.
The sequence at the crossing is clear enough,
but the reasoning behind it is still disputed.
This episode keeps to that position.
The times are less disputed. The State Department's note gives 10:30
in the morning on 28 October, Berlin time,
as the moment the Soviet tanks began withdrawing from the checkpoint.
The Stiftung Berliner Mauer says the Soviet Union withdrew
its tanks the next morning, after 16 hours.
Both put the pullback on the morning of 28 October.
They give slightly different starts, so this episode gives
the time only as the State Department records it.
Read together, the two sources describe the same
morning and the same order of events:
the Soviet tanks pulled back first, and the American tanks followed.
The Stiftung describes the ending in a few lines. In secret negotiations,
the two superpowers had agreed to end the sabre rattling,
and the American tanks followed shortly after the Soviet tanks had gone.
The State Department's note gives the start of the Soviet pullback,
but it does not describe the order in
which the tanks left the street.
Only one Wikipedia passage gives that order,
so it is not told here.
What the sources agree on is that the armour left,
and that the standoff was over.
The standoff had lasted about sixteen hours, from the late afternoon
of 27 October to the morning of 28 October.
By the morning of 28 October the armour was leaving the street,
and both sides had stepped back from the confrontation.
Consider what had been settled and what had not.
The tanks were gone.
Lightner had been turned back at the line over papers,
and the question of papers was the one the standoff began with.
Neither the Stiftung nor the State Department's note
says that this question was settled.
The sources do not show that the border guards' rule had changed,
so the crossing was still where it had always been.
What did that place look like once the armour had gone?
Yusuf again, one more thing before the story goes on.
If you can't join me in person,
my audio walks take you along the Berlin Wall at
Bernauer Straße and through the medieval old town,
at your own pace, on your phone.
They're at walk of berlin dot com.
Now the crossing as you find it. Start with the guardhouse.
The one standing on Friedrichstraße today is a replica.
Wikipedia says a copy of the guardhouse and of the sign
was reconstructed later, roughly on the same site,
and a German travel guide calls the wooden hut a replica.
It resembles the first guardhouse of 1961,
which stood behind a sandbag barrier.
What you see is a reconstruction on or near the old spot,
not the building that stood there in October.
Stand on the corner where the two streets meet,
and you are standing on the junction the Chronik names.
The difference matters when you read this story against the street,
so keep it in mind as you stand there.
The original guardhouse is somewhere else now.
A 1990 photo record from the Deutsche Kinemathek says the American
guardhouse was dismantled and is now in the Allied Museum.
Its caption says the little hut still stood
at the crossing on 4 June.
A photo record in the Allied Museum's collection on the museum-digital
database dates the dismantling to 22 June 1990,
and says the booth is in the museum's collection.
Wikipedia also says the original was removed
in 1990 and is now displayed there.
Two independent sources agree on where the hut ended up,
and two agree on the June date.
The sign has its own story.
A 1990 photo record from the Deutsche Kinemathek shows a sign
in four languages: English, Russian, French and German.
Its transcription gives the German line as Sie verlassen den amerikanischen Sektor,
which means you are leaving the American sector.
The record's transcription is partly garbled,
so this episode quotes only that German line.
Wikipedia says the sign outside today is a copy,
reconstructed with the guardhouse, and the German travel guide
describes it as a copy in four languages.
Stand in front of it and read the languages slowly.
The same warning is written in each one.
The Haus am Checkpoint Charlie stands on the same street,
at Friedrichstraße 43 to 45.
The Chronik der Mauer names it the Mauermuseum.
Its own page calls Checkpoint Charlie the best-known
crossing between West and East,
and its list of events for 13 August 1961 says armed GDR
units sealed off West Berlin and the construction of the Wall began.
Check the museum's website for current opening times before you go.
A large light box by the artist Frank Thiel stands at the
site, with a larger-than-life photograph of an American soldier,
and the Chronik der Mauer describes it as drawing attention to
the military presence of the Allies in Berlin.
The Allied Museum is not on Friedrichstraße.
It is at Clayallee 135, and the museum's own page offers visitors
the chance to enter the last guardhouse of Checkpoint Charlie.
The page lists general opening hours and separate times
for the large outdoor objects, but hours change,
so check the museum's website before you go.
Treat the Allied Museum as the place where the original hut stands,
and the street as the place where the standoff happened.
Both belong to the same story,
and a single visit lets you see the difference between them.
Look at the road surface as you walk.
visitBerlin describes a double row of paving stones that marks the
former course of the Wall in the street.
It shows where the border ran without needing a wall to
stand on. visitBerlin also calls Checkpoint Charlie one
of the best-known places on the Berlin Wall.
The Wall itself is no longer there,
which is why the marking matters. Where the line runs underfoot,
you are reading the border in the street itself,
not in a display case. Stand on it,
and you are standing on the line the Wall once followed,
as the marking says.
The Chronik der Mauer places another marker close by.
In Zimmerstraße, about 200 metres from the former Checkpoint Charlie,
a memorial column stands, with a line of bricks
that marks the path of the former Wall.
It is the Peter Fechter memorial.
Peter Fechter, aged 18, was shot by East German border guards and
bled to death at the Wall on 17 August 1962,
less than a year after the tanks left the street.
The federal agency for civic education records his
death in its account of the Wall.
Walk to the memorial and stand there for a moment.
The name matters more than the bricks, and it is the
sober way to end a walk along this line.
Here is what the record gives you, and what it does not.
The tanks, the figures and the times of the pullback
come from accounts that do not always agree,
and this episode has kept to the points where they do.
Two things are firm. The American and Soviet tanks faced each
other at Friedrichstraße on 27 October, and the Soviet tanks began
to leave on the morning of 28 October.
Everything else, from the number of tanks at midnight
to the order in which the tanks withdrew,
is a detail to check in the sources named along the way.
The Stiftung Berliner Mauer's website and the State Department's historical record
are the places to check a figure yourself.
Now the close. Stand at the corner where Friedrichstraße meets Zimmerstraße,
and look at the replica guardhouse first. Then read the sign.
Then look along the road for the double row of
paving stones that marks where the Wall ran.
The tanks that stood on this street in October 1961 are gone,
and the crossing that caused the standoff is
now a place of visits, photographs and displays.
The replica hut and the sign tell you what the crossing looks
like now, and the paving line tells you where the border ran.
Nothing you see there is the original scene.
But it is the street the sources name, and that is enough
to picture the night the armour came to Friedrichstraße.
Then go to Clayallee 135, and step inside the last
guardhouse of Checkpoint Charlie at the Allied Museum.
The museum's page invites visitors to enter it,
and two accounts identify it as the original hut.
Take a minute inside it, and think about how much depended on
a single set of papers at a checkpoint.
Four occupying powers, a divided city and a senior diplomat who
would not identify himself to a border guard:
the argument over those papers is what the whole episode turns on.
The record does not say for certain who ordered the tanks forward,
but the crossing is still there to stand in.
Stand there for a minute before you go.
That's this week's story.
I'm Yusuf, and if you want to stand where it happened,
my walks and audio walks are at walk of berlin dot com.
